title: Authentic Materials at Scale

pts: Authentic materials — real news, real podcasts, real workplace documents — expose learners to language exactly as it's actually used.
At B1–B2, learners are often ready to engage with more authentic input than a coursebook alone typically provides.
This directly extends Unit 13's coursebook-supplementing principles into a more substantial course design choice.

v: One coursebook unit; five real texts collected locally

items: Choose one coursebook unit you teach at B1–B2.
Collect five real English texts on the same topic: a notice, a news item, a label, an advertisement, a short video clip.
Compare them with the coursebook text: vocabulary, sentence length, layout, purpose, audience.
Note what the real texts offer that the coursebook does not.
Decide which one real text you would add, and why.
Learners bring real English texts from home or the market and the class sorts them by purpose.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An audit note for a Class 9 unit on health:

lines: Coursebook: a neat clinic dialogue. Real texts: a paracetamol strip label, a vaccination camp notice, a 90-second doctor’s interview on a news channel. Missing from the coursebook: abbreviations (tab., mg), imperatives in instructions, fast unscripted speech, formal notice layout.

blocks.x: The audit does not show that the coursebook is poor. It shows the particular gap that real texts can fill.

body: Purpose: to show the range of authentic English around learners. Content: an open coursebook surrounded by real texts from an Indian town: a bus ticket, a medicine strip, a cricket scoreboard, a shop sign in English and Kannada, a phone showing a news headline. Style: lively, documentary. Board version: a book with five labelled boxes around it.

items: A phone camera (free) to photograph real texts for later use.

blocks.x: A folder of tickets, labels, leaflets and newspaper cuttings.

points.h: Grading the Task, Not Just the Text
pts: Rather than simplifying an authentic text itself, grade the task around it — a simpler comprehension task on the same full text.
This preserves the text's authentic richness while still making it accessible at the right difficulty level.
This directly echoes Unit 13's principle: grade the task before grading the text.

items: Choose one authentic text, such as a short news report, and do not simplify it.
Prepare three tasks of increasing demand on it (see model language).
Everyone does task 1; most move to task 2; confident readers try task 3.
Check answers in pairs, then as a class.
Highlight two useful expressions that all learners can take away.
Groups do different tasks, then teach each other what they found.
Support: task 1 only, with a bilingual glossary of five key words.
Challenge: task 3, plus a two-sentence summary for a younger reader.

blocks.x: Text: a regional newspaper report on a lake clean-up (250–350 words).

lines: Task 1: Find three numbers in the text. What does each describe?
Task 2: Who organized the clean-up? What problem did they want to solve?
Task 3: Is the reporter neutral or on one side? Find two words that show this.

blocks.x: The text stays the same; the demand changes. This is the principle from Unit 13: grade the task before you grade the text (see also Nuttall 2005).

body: Purpose: to show task grading. Content: a newspaper page with three ladders of different heights leaning against it, labelled ‘Find’, ‘Understand’, ‘Evaluate’. Figures climb each, all reaching the same page. Style: diagrammatic. Board version: one rectangle and three ladders.

items: Breaking News English (free) when you do need the same story at several levels.

blocks.x: One copy of the article per bench, with the three tasks on the board.

body: Start with the easiest question that still requires reading the real text. Questions answerable from the headline or picture alone do not build reading skill.

pts: Build a growing bank of authentic materials organised by topic, level, and skill focus, rather than sourcing fresh material every single lesson.
Digital tools (Unit 18) make this collection and organisation far more manageable than it once was.
A systematic bank also supports consistency across a scheme of work (Unit 14).

v: 45 minutes to set up, then 10 minutes a week
A shared folder or box file; an index

items: Agree categories: topic, estimated level, skill focus, genre, source and permission status.
Create one sub-folder per topic from the scheme of work (Unit 14).
Each teacher adds two texts a month, each with an index line and one ready-made task.
Tag each text after use: ‘worked well’, ‘too hard’, ‘needs support’.
Review each term and remove out-of-date texts.
DIET or cluster teacher circles share banks across schools.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Topic: Water | Level: B1 | Skill: gist and detail | Genre: news report | Source: regional daily (date recorded) | Permission: classroom display only | Task: ‘Three numbers’ | Tag: worked well with 9A.

blocks.x: A bank grows slowly and saves time quickly: four teachers adding two texts a month have almost fifty after a term and a half.

body: Purpose: to show systematic organization. Content: a filing cabinet with drawers labelled Water, Health, Sport, Work, Festivals; one open drawer shows index cards with colour-coded level and skill tags. Style: tidy, practical. Board version: a table with column headings.

items: Google Drive (free) with a Google Sheets index.
Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for a visual bank by topic.

blocks.x: A labelled box file in the staffroom with an index notebook.

pts: Podcasts, interviews and video content expose learners to natural speech rate and connected speech (Unit 4) that scripted audio smooths away.
Select material with clear enough audio quality that the challenge is linguistic, not acoustic.
This connects directly to Unit 32's extensive listening principles, at a more intensively-taught scale.

v: A 2–3 minute authentic clip; speaker or phone

items: Check the clip in advance: clear sound, one or two speakers, a relatable topic.
First listening: one gist question.
Second listening: a short detail task.
Third listening, in short sections: learners notice connected speech in one or two transcribed sentences.
Pairs discuss the topic, using one expression they heard.
Use a local English-language radio interview, so learners hear fluent Indian English as a model.
Support: five key words before listening; a transcript for the third listening.
Challenge: predict the speaker’s next point at each pause.

lines: Written: We are going to try and get it done by the end of the month.
Heard: We’re gonna try ’n’ get it done by the end o’ the month.
T: How many words did you hear in ‘try and get it’?
S1: It sounds like one word.
T: Exactly. Real speech links words together. Once more.

blocks.x: Field (2008) argues that learners need practice in decoding real speech, not only in answering comprehension questions. This is the intensive counterpart of the extensive listening in Unit 32.

body: Purpose: to show connected speech. Content: a sentence as separate words at the top; below, the same sentence as one wave with linked sounds shown as bridges. Style: clean, audio-inspired. Board version: the sentence with linking arcs.

items: BBC Learning English (free) for interviews with transcripts.
YouTube (free) with captions, checked for accuracy before use.

blocks.x: The teacher reads a real interview transcript aloud at natural speed, then slowly.

pts: News articles, product reviews, and workplace emails each carry distinct genre conventions (Unit 33) worth exposing learners to directly.
Authentic reading complements, rather than replaces, the graded extensive reading programme from Unit 31.
Choose genres relevant to learners' real needs, informed by the needs analysis from Unit 2.

v: Four short authentic texts of different genres

items: Choose four genres that match learners’ needs (Unit 2): a product review, a job advertisement, a formal email, a news report.
Give each group one text without its source.
Groups identify genre, audience and purpose, and find three features that show this.
Each group reports in one minute.
Build a class chart of genre features for later writing (Unit 33).
Compare an Indian and a non-Indian text in the same genre.
Support: a checklist of features (greeting, headline, star rating, bullets).
Challenge: rewrite a short text in a different genre.

lines: Product review: star rating, first person, I’d definitely recommend…, a short verdict.
Job advertisement: We are looking for…, bulleted requirements, a closing date.
Formal email: I am writing to…, Kind regards.

blocks.x: Authentic reading complements the graded extensive reading programme in Unit 31; it does not replace it.

body: Purpose: to show that genres have recognizable shapes. Content: four page outlines: a review with stars, a job advertisement with a bullet list, an email with greeting and sign-off, a news report with headline and columns. Key features are circled. Style: minimal line drawings. Board version: four quick outlines.

items: Newsela (free basic access; some features paid) for news at several levels. [VERIFY current free-tier availability in India]

blocks.x: Newspaper cuttings, printed advertisements and letters.

pts: Using authentic materials at scale raises real copyright considerations that occasional classroom use often escapes notice of.
Favour openly licensed or clearly permitted sources for materials that will be reused or distributed repeatedly.
Institutional guidance should inform this practice; it varies meaningfully across contexts.

items: For each text, note the source and any stated licence (for example Creative Commons).
Sort into three groups: openly licensed; free to view but copyright reserved; unclear.
Decide how each group can be used: shown in class, linked, or printed and distributed.
Replace ‘unclear’ texts you plan to copy in bulk with openly licensed alternatives.
Agree a simple school policy with a school leader or DIET faculty member.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A decision guide (written for this book, not legal advice):

lines: Openly licensed (e.g. CC BY): copy and adapt with attribution.
Free to view, copyright reserved: show or link; avoid bulk printing.
Unclear: treat as copyright reserved.

blocks.x: India’s Copyright Act 1957 permits certain educational uses, but their scope is not always clear to non-lawyers [VERIFY current interpretation of section 52 for classroom copying]. Institutional guidance should decide practice.

body: Purpose: to make permissions memorable. Content: three lights: green ‘Openly licensed: copy with credit’, amber ‘Free to view: show or link’, red ‘Unclear: do not copy in bulk’. Style: bold, simple. Board version: three circles.

items: StoryWeaver by Pratham Books (free, openly licensed stories in English and Indian languages).
Creative Commons search tools (free) for openly licensed texts and images.

blocks.x: A printed permissions checklist kept with the text bank.

pts: Authentic material doesn't arrive pre-graded to a CEFR level — evaluating and calibrating difficulty is a genuine skill to build.
Readability tools and vocabulary-frequency checks (Unit 5) support this evaluation, though judgement still matters.
Expect more variance in difficulty across authentic materials than a graded coursebook, and plan support accordingly.

v: One authentic text; a frequency profiler

items: Run the text through a vocabulary profiler, or mark by hand words learners probably do not know.
Estimate the percentage of known words.
Consider sentence length, background knowledge, layout support and topic familiarity.
Decide: use as it is, with pre-teaching, with a lighter task, or not at all.
After the lesson, record whether your estimate was accurate.
Two teachers rate the same text independently and compare.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Text: a 300-word mobile phone review. About 20 words fall outside the most frequent 2,000 word families, including ‘processor’ and ‘refresh rate’. Background knowledge: high. Decision: pre-teach six words; use with a B1 task.

blocks.x: Coverage figures are a guide, not a rule: a familiar topic makes a text easier than its word list suggests (Nation 2013).

body: Purpose: to show that difficulty has several parts. Content: a balance scale; one side holds ‘unknown words’, ‘long sentences’, ‘unfamiliar topic’; the other ‘pictures’, ‘familiar topic’, ‘pre-teaching’, ‘lighter task’. Style: clean. Board version: a simple scale.

items: Lextutor VocabProfile (free) for a frequency breakdown.
Text Inspector (limited free use; full version paid) for an estimated CEFR profile.

blocks.x: Underline unknown words on a printed copy and count them per hundred words.

body: Comprehension tends to drop noticeably when learners know much less than about 95 per cent of the running words (Hu and Nation 2000). One unknown word in twenty sounds small, but in a 300-word text it means about fifteen.

pts: A course built substantially around authentic materials still benefits from some prepared, structured input, especially for explicit language focus.
This is a balance, not a wholesale replacement of everything Tier I's coursebook principles established.
Plan the proportion deliberately at the scheme-of-work level (Unit 14), rather than let it happen by accident.

v: Scheme of work for one term (Unit 14)

items: List the weeks of the term.
For each week, mark the main input source: coursebook, authentic text, or both.
Mark where explicit language focus happens and what material supports it.
Check the balance: a steady flow of authentic material, with explicit focus still protected.
Adjust so that the proportion is a decision, not an accident.
Map two classes of the same grade and compare the balance each needs.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Week 1: coursebook reading + authentic notice. Focus: imperatives (coursebook).
Week 2: authentic podcast clip + coursebook page on reported speech.
Week 3: authentic news report + teacher-made vocabulary sheet.
Week 4: project week using the text bank.

blocks.x: Tomlinson (2011) describes good materials as balancing exposure to real language with opportunities to notice and practise it.

body: Purpose: to show a planned proportion. Content: a ten-week timeline; each week is a bar in two colours, authentic and prepared, with proportions varying but never falling to zero. Style: clean chart. Board version: ten shaded boxes.

items: Google Sheets (free) with colour-coded weeks.

blocks.x: A term grid in the planning notebook, drawn with two pen colours.

body: This term, add one authentic text a week to one class, with a graded task rather than a simplified text. After six weeks, add the texts that worked to your bank and share them with a colleague.

dek: Unit 41 of 100: extending Tier I's coursebook adaptation into a course substantially built from real-world texts — with the extra grading and management that requires.

aims.x: This unit moves from the occasional authentic supplement described in Unit 13 to a course built substantially around real-world texts: news reports, podcasts, interviews, reviews, notices and workplace emails. It shows how to keep such texts accessible by grading the task, how to build a bank of materials, and how to handle copyright and uneven difficulty.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what authenticity means and why it matters at B1–B2;
grade tasks so that learners can work with unsimplified texts;
build and organize a shared bank of authentic materials;
exploit authentic audio and video for intensive listening;
match authentic reading genres to learners’ needs;
apply basic copyright caution and prefer openly licensed sources;
estimate the difficulty of an authentic text using tools and judgement;
plan a deliberate balance of authentic and prepared material.

why: Why this matters. Occasional authentic material supplements a coursebook. Building a course substantially around it is a bigger commitment — and a natural fit for Tier II's integration focus.

background.x: In its simplest sense, an authentic text is one produced for a real audience and purpose, not for language learners. Henry Widdowson (1978) distinguished the genuineness of a text, a property of the text itself, from its authenticity, which depends on how a reader engages with it. A genuine newspaper article can be used in a thoroughly inauthentic way, for example to hunt for past tense verbs. Alex Gilmore’s (2007) review concluded that authentic materials can support communicative competence, especially awareness of how language varies with context, but that their value depends heavily on the tasks built around them.

At B1–B2 many learners have outgrown the tidy English of coursebook dialogues. They need to meet the hesitations and connected speech of real talk (Unit 4), the conventions of real genres (Unit 33), and the vocabulary that actually occurs in the world. Research on vocabulary coverage suggests that learners generally need to know around 95–98 per cent of the running words in a text to read it with adequate comprehension (Hu and Nation 2000; Nation 2013). Authentic texts rarely meet that threshold for intermediate learners, which is why task design and careful selection become central skills.

In India, authentic English surrounds learners even where it is rarely spoken at home: bus tickets, medicine labels, cricket commentary, packaging, government notices and bank SMS alerts. Many of these texts also exist in Kannada, Hindi, Tamil or other languages, which gives teachers parallel material and a bridge from the home language. The NEP 2020 encourages experiential learning and the use of home languages (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and the NCF 2023 stresses that language learning should connect with learners’ lives beyond school (NCERT 2023). This unit is not an argument against coursebooks; it is an argument for choosing the proportion of real-world text deliberately.

items: Graded-task performance. Compare success on three task levels using the same authentic text.
Genre recognition. Learners name the genre, audience and three features of an unseen text.
Listening decoding. A short dictation from a real clip, marked for words correctly identified.
Learner response. A brief survey: ‘Which real texts helped you most? Which were too hard?’
What proportion of the English your learners meet in class is authentic?
When you last simplified a text, could you have graded the task instead?
Which real English texts in your learners’ environment have you not yet used?
How do you judge whether an authentic text is too hard?
What would a shared text bank need to work in your school or cluster?

terms.def: A text, recording or object created for real communication rather than for language teaching, such as a bus timetable, a newspaper report or a product label.
The quality of being genuine in origin or use: a text may be authentic because it was written for real communication, and a task may be authentic because it reflects what learners do outside class.
Natural, fluent speech in which sounds in neighbouring words change, link or disappear, as when want to becomes wanna; learners need practice in hearing it.
A type of text with a recognized social purpose and typical stages and language, such as a recount, a complaint letter, a lab report or a nursing handover.
A property of a text produced for a real audience and purpose, not for learners. Widdowson (1978) distinguished it from authenticity, which depends on how a reader engages with the text.
A licence, such as Creative Commons, that allows others to reuse, adapt and share material freely under stated conditions, such as crediting the author.

How easy a text is to read for a particular group of learners, shaped by vocabulary, sentence length, organization, topic familiarity and layout. Formulas give a rough estimate, but a teacher’s judgement of the class remains essential.

Adjusting the difficulty of a task, rather than the text, to suit learners’ level, for example asking lower-level learners to find three facts and more advanced learners to evaluate the writer’s argument using the same text.
A shared, organized collection of texts, graded and labelled by level, topic and genre, which teachers build and draw on for teaching. A staffroom text bank can include a permissions checklist.
The proportion of words in a text that a reader knows, used to judge whether a text suits a learner’s level. Extensive reading generally needs very high coverage, around 98 per cent (Nation 2006).
